If thou bee'st fast to thy self.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I hope I shall be:
And your Example will work more.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Thou shalt not want it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: How do you, Sir? Can you lend a Man an Angel?
I hear you let out Money.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Very well, Sir,
You are pleasantly dispos'd: I am glad to see it,
Can you lend me your patience, and be rul'd by me?

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Is't come to Patience now?

speeches.speaker: Arch.
verse: Is't not a vertue?

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: I know nor. I ne're found it so.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: That's because
Thy Anger ever knows, and not thy Judgment.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: I know you have been rifl'd.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Nothing less, Boy:
Lord, What Opinions these vain People publish?
Rifl'd of what?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Study your Vertue, patience,
It may get Mustard to your Meat. Why in such haste, Sir,
Sent ye for me?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: For this end only, Theodore,
To wait upon your Sisters to the Court;
I am commanded they live there.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Toth' Court, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Toth' Court, I say.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: And must I wait upon 'em?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Yes, 'tis most fit ye should, ye are their Brother.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Is this the Business? I had thought your mind, Sir,
Had been set forward on some noble Action,
Something had truly stirr'd ye. Toth' Court with these?
Why, they are your Daughters, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: All this I know, Sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: The good old Woman on a Bed he threw.
To th' Court?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Thou art not mad.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Nor drunk as you are:
Drunk with your duty, Sir: Do you call it Duty?
A Pox o' duty, what can these do there?
What should they do? Can ye look Babies, Sisters
In the young Gallants eyes, and twirl their Band-strings?
Can ye ride out to air your selves? Pray, Sir,
Be serious with me: Do you speak this truly?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Why, didst thou never hear of Women
Yet at Court, boy?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Yes, and good Women too, very good Women,
Excellent honest Women; but are you sure, Sir,
That these will prove so?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: There's the danger, Brother.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: God a mercy Wench, thou hast a grudging of it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Now be you serious, Sir, and observe what I say,
Do it, and do it handsomly; go with 'em.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: With all my heart, Sir; I am in no Fault now;
If they be thought Whores for being in my Company;
Pray write upon their backs, they are my Sisters,
And where I shall deliver 'em.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Ye are wondrous Jocund,
But prethee tell me, art thou so lewd a Fellow,
I never knew thee fail a truth.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am a Soldier,
And spell ye what that means.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: A Soldier? What dost thou make of me?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Your Pallat's down, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar
verse: I thank ye, Sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Come, shall we to this matter?
You will to Court?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: If you will please to honour us.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I'le honour ye, I warrant: I'le set yee off
With such a lustre, Wenches: Alas, poor Viola,
Thou art a Fool, thou criest for eating White-bread:
Be a good House-wife of thy Tears, and save 'em,
Thou wilt have time enough to shed 'em, Sister.
Do you weep too? Nay, then I'le fool no more.
Come, worthy Sisters, since it must be so,
And since he thinks it fit to try your Vertues,
Be you as strong to Truth, as I to guard ye,
And this old Gentleman shall have joy of ye.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Burris take you ten thousand of those Crowns,
And those two Chains of Pearl they hold the richest,
I give 'em ye.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I humbly thank your Grace;
And may your great Example work in me
That noble Charity to Men more worthy,
And of more Wants.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: You bear a good mind, Burris;
Take twenty thousand now; Be not so modest,
It shall be so, I give 'em; go, there's my Ring for't.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Heaven bless your Highness ever.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: You are honest.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: They're coming now to Court, as fair as Vertue:
Two brighter Stars ne're rose here.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Peace, I have it,
And what my Art can do; the Duke —

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I am gone,
Remember.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I am counsell'd to the full, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: My pretty Mistress, whether lyes your Business?
How kindly I should take this, were it to me now?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I must confess immediately to your Grace,
At this time.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You have no Address, I do believe ye,
I would ye had.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: 'Twere too much Boldness, Sir;
Upon so little Knowledge, less deserving.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You'll make a perfect Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: a very poor one.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: A very fair one, Sweet: come hither to me.
What killing Eyes this Wench has? in his Glory
Not the bright Sun, when the Sirian Star reigns,
Shines half so fiery.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Why does your Grace so view me?
Nothing but common Handsomness dwells here, Sir,
Scarce that: your Grace is pleas'd to mock my meanness.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thou shalt not go: I do not lie unto thee,
In my Eye thou appear'st —

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Dim not the sight, Sir,
I am too dull an Object.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Canst thou love me?
Canst thou love him will honour thee?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I can love,
And love as you do too: but 'twill not shew well:
Or if it do shew here where all Light lustres,
Tinsel Affections, make a glorious glistering,
'Twill halt i' th' handsome way.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Are ye so cunning?
Dost think I love not truly?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: No, ye cannot,
You never travell'd that way yet: pray pardon me,
I prate so boldly to you.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: There's no harm done:
But what's your reason, Sweet?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I would tell your Grace,
But happily —

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: It shall be pleasing to me.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I should love you again, and then you would hate me,
With all my Service I should follow ye,
And through all Dangers.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: This would more provoke me,
More make me see thy Worths,
More make me meet 'em.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You should do so, if ye did well and truly.
But though ye be a Prince, and have Power in ye,
Power of Example too, ye have fail'd and falter'd.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Give me Example where?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You had a Mistress,
Oh Heaven, so bright, so brave a Dame, so lovely,
In all her Life so true.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: A Mistress?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That serv'd ye with that Constancy, that Care,
That lov'd your Will, and woo'd it too

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What Mistress?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That nurs'd your Honour up, held fast your Vertue;
And when she kiss'd encreas'd, not stole your Goodness.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And I neglected her?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Lost her, forsook her,
Wantonly flung her off.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What was her Name?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Her Name as lovely as her self, as noble,
And in it all that's excellent.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What was it?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Her Name was Beau-desert
Do you know her now, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Beau-desert? I not remember —

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I know you do not:
Yet she has a plainer Name; Lord Archas Service;
Do you yet remember her? there was a Mistress!
Fairer than Women, far fonder to you, Sir,
Than Mothers to their first-born Joys: Can you love?
Dare you profess that Truth to me a Stranger,
A thing of no Regard, no Name, no Lustre,
When your most noble Love you have neglected,
A Beauty all the World would woo and honour?
Would you have me credit this? think ye can love me,
And hold ye constant, when I have read this Story?
Is't possible you should ever favour me,
To a slight Pleasure prove a Friend, and fast too,
When, where you were most ty'd, most bound to benefit,
Bound by the Chains of Honesty and Honour,
You have broke and boldly too? I am a weak one,
Arm'd only with my Fears: I beseech your Grace
Tempt me no further.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Who taught you this Lesson?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Woful Experience, Sir: If you seek a Fair one,
Worthy your Love, if yet you have that perfect,
Two Daughters of his ruin'd Vertue now
Arrive at Court, excellent fair indeed, Sir;
But this will be the Plague on't, they're excellent honest.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I love thy Face.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Upon my Life ye cannot.
I do not love it my self, Sir, 'tis a lewd one,
So truly ill, Art cannot mend it; for if 'twere handsome,
At least if I thought so, you should hear me talk, Sir,
In a new Strain; and though ye are a Prince,
Make ye petition to me too, and wait my Answers;
Yet, o'my Conscience, I should pity ye
After some Ten years Siege.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Prithee do now.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: What would ye do?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why I would lye with ye.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I do not think ye would.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: In troth I would, Wench.
Here, take this Jewel.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Out upon't that's scurvy.
Nay, if we do, sure we'll do for good Fellowship,
For pure Love, or nothing: thus you shall be sure, Sir,
You shall not pay too dear for't.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Sure I cannot.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: By'r Lady but ye may: when ye have found me able
To do your Work well, ye may pay my Wages.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why does your Grace start back?

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: I ha' seen that shakes me:
Chills all my Blood: O where is Faith or Goodness?
Alinda thou art false, false thou fair one,
Wickedly false; and (woe is me) I see it.
For ever false.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I am glad 't has taken thus right.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I'll go ask my Lady, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Whether I shall lye with you, or no: If I find her willing—
For look ye, Sir, I have sworn, while I am in her Service—
('Twas a rash Oath I must confess.)

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thou mockest me.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Why, would you lye with me, if I were willing?
Would you abuse my Weakness?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I would piece it,
And make it stronger.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I humbly thank your Highness,
When you piece me, you must pice me to my Coffin:
When you have got my Maiden-head, I take it,
'Tis not an Inch of an Ape's Tail will restore it;
I love you, and I honour you; but this way
I'll neither love nor serve you:
Heaven change your Mind, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And thine too:
For it must be chang'd, it shall be.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: They are goodly Gentlewomen.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: They are,
Wondroos sweet Women both.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Does your Lordship like 'em?
They are my Sisters, Sir; good lusty Lasses,
They'll do their Labour well, I warrant you
You'll find no Bed-straw here, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Thank you, Brother.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: this is not so strongly built; but she is good Mettle,
Of a good stirring strain too: she goes tith, Sir.
Here they be, Gentlemen, must make you merry,
The Toys you wot of: do you like their Complexions?
They be no Moors: what think you of this Hand, Gentlemen?
Here's a white Altar for your Sacrifice:
A thousann Kisses here. Nay, keep off yet, Gentlemen,
Let's start first, and have fair Play: what would you give now
To turn the Globe up, and find the rich Moluccas?
To pass the Straights? Here (do you itch) by St. Nicholas,
Here's that will make you scratch and claw,
Claw my fine Gentlemen, move you in divers sorts:
Pray you let me request you to forget
To say your Prayers, whilst these are Courtiers;
Or if you needs will think of Heaven, let it be no higher
Than their Eyes?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: How will you have 'em bestow'd, Sir?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Even how your Lordship please,
So you do not bake 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Bake 'em!

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They are too high a Meat that way, they run to Gelly.
But if you'll have 'em for your own Diet, take my Counsel,
Stew 'em between two Feather-beds.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Please you, Colonel,
To let 'em wait upon the Princess?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Yes, Sir,
And thank your Honour too: But then happily,
These noble Gentlemen shall have no access to 'em;
And to have 'em buy new Cloaths, study new Faces,
And keep a stinking stir with themselves for nothing,
'Twill not be well i'saith; they have kept their Bodies,
And bin at charge for Baths: Do you see that Shirt there?
Weigh but the moral meaning, 'twill be grievous:
Alas I brought them to delight these Gentlemen,
I weigh their wants by mine: I brought 'em wholesome,
Wholesome, and young, my Lord, and two such Blessings.
They will not light upon again in Ten years.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: 'Tis fit they wait upon her.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They are fit for any thing.
They'll wait upon a Man, they are not bashful,
Carry his Cloak, or untie his Points, or any thing,
Drink drunk, and take Tobacco; the familiar'st Fools—.
This Wench will leap over Stools too, and sound a Trumpet,
Wrastle, and pitch the Bar; they are finely brought up,

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ladies, you are bound to your Brother,
And have much cause to thank him:
Ile ease you of this Charge, and to the Princess,
So please you, Ile attend 'em.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thank your Lordship:
If there be e'er a private Corner as you go Sir,
A foolish Lobby out oth' way, make danger,
Try what they are, try.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ye are a merry Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I would fain be your Honours Kinsman.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ye are too curst Sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Farewel Wenches, keep close your Ports y'are washt else.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Brother bestow your Fears where they are needful.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Honor thy Name is, and I hope thy Nature.
Goe after, Gentlemen, goe, get a Snatch if you can,
Yond' old Erra Pater will never please 'em,
Alas I brought 'em for you, but see the luck on't,
I swear I meant as honestly toward ye—
Nay do not cry good Gentlemen: a little Counsel
Will do no harm: they'll walk abroad ith' Evenings,
Ye may surprize 'em easily, they wear no Pistols.
Set down your Minds in Metre, flowing Metre,
And get some good old Linnen Woman to deliver it,
That has the trick on't: you cannot fail:
Farewel Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: You have frighted off the Flesh flies.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Flesh flies indeed my Lord.
And it must be very stinking Flesh they will not seize on.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Your Lordship bid me bring this Casket.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Yes. Cood Colonel
Commend me to your worthy Father, and as a Pledge
He ever holds my Love and Service to him,
Deliver him this poor but hearty Token,
And where I may be his.—

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Ye are too Noble;
A Wonder here my Lord, that dare be Honest,
When all Men hold it Vitious: I shall deliver it,
And with it your most Noble Love. Your Servant.
Were there but two more such at Court, 'rwere Sainted,
This will buy Brawn this Christmas yet, and Muscadine.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Broom. Broom, the bonny Broom,
Come buy my Birchen Broom,
Ith' wars we have no more room,
Buy all my bonny Broom.
For a Kiss take two;
If those will not do,
For a little, little Pleasure,
Take all my whole Treasure:
If all those will not do't,
Take the Broom-man to boot.
Broom, Broom, the bonny Broom.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: The Wars are done and gone,
And Soldiers now neglected, Pedlars are,
Come Maidens, come alone,
For I can shew you handsom, handsome Ware.
Powders for the Hoad,
And Drinks for your Bed,
To make ye blith and bonny.
As well in the Night we Soldiers can fight,
And please a young Wench as any.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: I have fine Potatos,
Ripe Potatos.

speeches.speaker: 3 Sol.
verse: Will ye buy any Honesty, come away,
I sell it openly by day,
I bring no forced light, nor no Candle
To cozen ye; come buy and handle:
This will shew the great Man Good,
The Tradsman where he swears and lyes,
Each Lady of a noble Blood,
The City Dame to rule her Eyes:
Ye are rich Men now: come buy, and then
Ile make ye richer, honest Men.

speeches.speaker: 4 Sol.
verse: Have ye any crackt Maiden-heads, to new leach or mend?
Have ye any old Maiden-heads to sell or to change?
Bring 'em to me, with a little pritty Gin,
Ile clout 'em, Ile mend 'em, Ile knock in a Pin,
Shall make 'em as good Maids agen,
As ever they have bin.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: What means all this, why do y'sell Brooms Ancient?
Is it Wantonness or Want?

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: The only Reason is,
To sweep your Lordships Conscience: here's one for the nonce.
Gape Sir, you have swallowed many a goodlier Matter—
The only casting for a crazy Conscience.

speeches.speaker: 3 Sol.
verse: Will your Lordship buy any Honesty? 'twilt be worth your Money

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: How is this?

speeches.speaker: 3 Sol.
verse: Honesty my Lord, 'tis here in a Quill.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Take heed you open it not, for 'tis so subtle,
The least puff of Wind will blow it out oth'Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: Will your Lordship taste a fine Potato?
'Twill advance your wither'd State.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Fill your Honour full of most noble Itches,
And make Jack dance in your Lordships Breeches.
prose:
If your Daughters on their Beds,
Have bow'd, or crackt their Maiden-heads;
If in a Coach with too much tumbling,
They chance to cry, fie, so, what fumbling;
If her Foot slip, and down fall she,
And break her Leg above the Knee,
The One and Thirtieth of February let this be tane,
And they shall be arrant Maids again.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ye are brave Soldiers; keep your wantonness,
A Winter will come on to shake this wilfulness.
Disport you selves, and when you want your Money —

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Broom, Broom, &c.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You must not be so fearful, little one,
Nor Lady you so sad, you will ne're make Courtiers
With these dull sullen Thoughts; this Place is pleasure,
Perserv'd to that use, so inhabited;
And those that live here, live delightful, joyful:
These are the Gardens of Adonis, Ladies,
Where all sweets to their free and noble Uses,
Grow ever young and courted.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Bess me Heaven,
Can things of her years arrive at these Rudiments?
By your leave fair Gentlewoman, how long have you bin here?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Faith much about a Week.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: You have studied hard,
And by my faith arriv'd at a great Knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Were not you bashful at first?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Ay, ay, for an Hour or two:
But when I saw People laugh'd at me for it,
And thought it a dull Breeding —

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: You are govern'd here then
Much after the Men's Opinions.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Ever Lady

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: And what they think is honourable.—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Most precisely
We follow with all Faith.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: A goodly Cathechism.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: But bashful for an Hour or two?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Faith to say true.
I do not think I was so long: for look ye,
'Tis to no end here, put on what shape ye will,
And sour your self with ne're so much Austerity,
You shall be courted in the same, and won too,
'Tis but some two Hours more; and so much time lost,
Which we hold precious here: In so much time now
As I have told you this, you may lose a Servant,
Your Age, nor all your Art can e'er recover.
Catch me occasion as she comes, hold fast there
Till what you do affect is ripn'd to ye.
Has the Duke seen ye yet?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: What if he have not?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You do your Beauties too much wrong, appearing
So full of sweetness, newness; set so richly,
As if a Council beyond Nature fram'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: If we were thus? say Heaven had given these Blessings,
Must we turn these to sin Oblations?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How foolishly this Country way shews in ye?
How full of Flegm? do you come here to pray Ladies.
You had best cry, stand away, let me alone Gentlemen,
Ile tell my Father else.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: This Woman's naught sure,
A very naughty Woman.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Come, say on friend,
Ile be instructed by ye.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You'll thank me for't.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Either I or the Devil shall: The Duke you were speaking of.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: 'Tis well remember'd: yes, let him first see you,
Appear not openly till he has view'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: He's a very Noble Prince they say.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: O wondrous gracious;
And as you may deliver your self at the first viewing;
For look ye, you must bear your self; yet take heed
It be so season'd with a sweet Humility,
And grac'd with such a Bounty in your Beauty—

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: But I hope he will offer me no ill?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: No, no:
Tis like he will kiss ye, and play with ye:

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Play with me, how?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Why, good Lord, that you are such a Fool now.
No harm assure your self.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Will ye play with me too?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Look Babies in your Eyes, my pretty sweet one:
There's a fine Sport: do you know your Lodgings yet?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: I hear of none.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I do then, they are handsome,
Convenient for access.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Access?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Yes little one,
For Visitation of those Friends and Servants,
Your Beauties shall make choice of: Friends and Visits:
Do you not know those uses? Alas poor Novice;
There's a close Couch or two, handsomely placed too.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: What are those I pray you?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Who would be troubled with such raw things? they are to lye upon,
And your Love by you; and discourse, and toy in.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Alas I have no Love.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You must by any means:
You'll have a Hundred, fear not.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Honesty keep me:
What shall I do with all those?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You'll find uses:
You are ignorant yet, let Time work; you must learn too,
To lie handsomly in your Bed a Mornings, neatly drest
In a most curious Wastcoat, to set you off well,
Play with your Bracelets, Sing; you must learn to Rhime too,
And Riddle neatly; study the hardest Language,
And 'tis no matter whether it be Sense or no,
So it go seemly off. Be sure you profit
In kissing, kissing sweetly: there lies a main Point,
A Key that opens to all practick Pleasure;
Ile help you to a Friend of mine shall teach you,
And suddenly: your Country way is fulsome.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Have you Schools for all these Mysteries?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: O yes,
And several Hours prefix'd to Study in:
You may have Kalanders to know the good Hour,
And when to take a Jewel: for the Ill too,
When to refuse, with Observations on 'em;
Under what Sign 'tis best meeting in an Arbor,
And in what Bower, and Hour it works; a Thousand,
When in a Coach, when in a private Lodging,
With all their Vertues.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Have you studied these?
How beastly they become your Youth? how bawdily?
A Woman of your tenderness, a Teacher,
Teacher of these lewd Arts? of your full Beauty?
A Man made up in Lust, would loath this in you:
The rankest Leacher, hate such Impudence.
They say the Devil can assume Heavens brightness,
And so appear to tempt us: sure thou art no Woman.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I joy to find thee thus.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Thou hast no tenderness,
No reluctation in thy Heart: 'tis mischief.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: All's one for that; read these and then be satisfy'd,
A few more private Rules I have gather'd for you,
Read 'em, and well observe 'em: so I leave you.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: A wondrous wicked Woman: shame go with thee

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: What new Pandoras Box is this? Ile see it,
Though presently I tear it. Read thine Viola,
'Tis in our own Wills to believe and follow.
How's this? Read yours out Sister: this amazes me.
prose:
Worthy Honora, as you have begun
In Vertues spotless School, so forward run.
Pursue that nobleness, and chaste desire
You ever had, burn in that holy Fire;
And a white Martyr to fair memory
Give up your Name, unsoil'd of Infamy.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Fear not thou yet unblasted Violet,
Nor let my wanton words a Doubt beget.
Live in that peace and sweetness of thy Bud,
Remember whose thou art, and grow still good.
Remember whose thou art, and stand a Story
Fit for thy noble Sex, and thine own Glory.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: I know not what to think.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Sure a good Woman,
An excellent Woman, Sister.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: It confounds me;
Let 'em use all their Arts, if these be their ends,
The Court I say breeds the best Foes and Friends.
Come, let's be honest Wench, and do our best service.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: A most excellent Woman, I will love her.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: MAdam, the Duke has sent for the two Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: I prethee go: I know thy Thoughts are with him.
Go, go Alinda, do not mock me more.
I have found thy Heart Wench, do not wrong thy Mistriss,
Thy too much loving Mistriss: do not abuse her.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: By your own fair Hands I understand you not.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: By thy own fair Eyes I understand thee too much,
Too far, and build a Faith there thou hast ruind.
Go, and enjoy thy Wish, thy Youth, thy Pleasure,
Enjoy the Greatness no doubt he has promised,
Enjoy the service of all Eyes that see thee,
The Glory thou hast aim'd at, and the triumph:
Only this last Love I ask, forget thy Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: O, who has wrong'd me? who has ruin'd me?
Poor wretched Girl, what poyson is flung on thee?
Excellent Vertue, from whence flows this Anger?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Go, ask my Brother, ask the Faith thou gav'st me,
Ask all my Favours to thee, ask my Love,
Last, thy forgetfulness of Good: then fly me,
For we must part Alinda.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You are weary of me;
I must confess, I was never worth your Service,
Your bounteous Favours less; but that my Duty,
My ready Will, and all I had to serve you—
O Heaven thou know'st my Honesty.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: No more:
Take heed, Heaven has a Justice: take this Ring with you,
This doting Spell you gave me: too well Alinda,
Thou know'st the Vertue in't; too well I feel it:
Nay keep that too, it may sometimes remember you,
When you are willing to forget who gave it,
And to what Vertuous end.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Must I go from you?
Of all the Sorrows sorrow has—must I part with you?
Part with my noble Mistress?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Or I with thee Wench.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: And part stain'd with Opinion? Farewel Lady,
Happy and Blessed Lady, goodness keep you:
Thus your poor Servant full of Grief turns from you,
For ever full of Grief, for ever from you.
I have no being now, no Friends, no Country,
I wander Heaven knows whither, Heaven knows how.
No Life, now you are lost: only mine innocence,
That little left me of my self, goes with me,
That's all my Bread and Comfort. I confess Madam,
Truly confess, the Duke has often courted me.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: And powr'd his Soul into thee, won thee.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Do you think so?
Well, time that told this Tale, will tell my truth too,
And say you had a faithful, honest Servant:
The business of my Life is now to pray for you,
Pray for your Vertuous Loves; Pray for your Children,
When Heaven shall make you happy.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: How she wounds me?
Either I am undone, or she must go: take these with you,
Some Toys may do you service; and this Money:
And when you want, I Love you not so poorly,
Not yet Alinda, that I would see you perish.
Prethee be good, and let me hear: look on me,
I Love those Eyes yet dearly; I have kiss'd thee,
And now Ile do't again: farewel Alinda,
I am too full to speak more, and too wretched.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You have my Faith,
And all the World my Fortune.

speeches.speaker: The:
verse: I would fain hear
What becomes of these two Wenches:
And if I can, I will do 'em good.
Do you hear my honest Friend?
He knows no such Name:
What a World of business,
Which by Interpretation are meer nothing,
These things have here? 'Mass now I think on't better,
I wish he be not sent for one of them
To some of these By-lodgings: methought I saw
A kind of Reference in his Face to Bawdery.
He has her, but 'tis none of them: hold fast thief:
An excellent touzing Knave. Mistress
You are to suffer your penance some half Hour hence now
How far a fine Court Custard with Plumbs in it
Will prevail with one of these waiting Gentlewomen,
They are taken with these soluble things exceedingly;
This is some Yeomen oth' Bottles now that has sent for her,
That she calls Father: now woe to this Ale incense.
By your leave Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Well Sir; what's your pleasure with me?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: You do not know the way to the Maid's Lodgings?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes indeed do I Sir,

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: But you will not tell me?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: No indeed will not I, because you doubt it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: These are fine Gim-cracks: hey, here comes another,
A Bottle of Wine in's Hand, I take it.
Well met my Friend, is that Wine?

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Yes indeed is it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Faith I'll drink on't then.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Ye may, because ye have sworn, SIr.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: 'Tis very good, I'll drink a great deal now, Sir.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: I cannot help it, Sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I'll drink more yet.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: 'Tis in your own Hands.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: There's your Bottle, I thank you.
Pray let me drink again.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Faith but ye shall not.
Now have I sworn, I take it. Fare you well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: This is the fin'st Place to live in I e'er ente'rd.
Here comes a Gentlewoman, and alone; I'll to her.
Madam, my Lord my Master —

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Who's your Lord, Sir?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: The Lord Boroskie, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Pray excuse me:
Here's something for your Pains: within this hour, Sir,
One of the choice young Ladies shall attend him:
Pray let it be in that Chamber juts out to the Water;
'Tis private and convenient: Do my humble Service
To my honourable good Lord, I beseech you, Sir;
If it please you to visit a poor Lady —
You carry the 'haviour of a noble Gentleman,

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I shall be bold.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: 'Tis a good Aptness in you.
I lye here in the Wood-yard, the blew Lodgings, Sir;
They call me merrily the Lady of the — Sir;
A little I know what belongs to a Gentleman,
And if it please you take the Pains.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Dear Lady, take the Pains?
Why a Horse would not take the Pains that thou requir'st now,
To cleave old Crab tree? One of the choice young Ladies!
I would I had let this Bawd go, she has frighted me;
I am cruelly afraid of one of my Tribe now;
But if they will do, the Devil cannot stop 'em.
Why should he have a young Lady? are Women now
O' th' Nature of Bottles, to be stopt with Corks?
O the thousand little Furies that fly here now!
How now, Captain?

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: I come to seek you out, Sir,
And all the Town I have travell'd.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What's the News, Man?

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: That, that concerns us all, and very nearly:
The Duke this Night holds a great Feast at Court,
To which he bids for Guests all his old Counsellors,
And all his Favourites: your Father's sent for.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Why he is neither in Coucil, nor in Favour.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: That's it: have an Eye now, or never, and a quick one,
An Eye that must not wink from good-Intelligence.
I heard a Bitd sing, they mean him no good Office.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Art sure he sups here?

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Sure as 'tis Day.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: 'Tis like then:
How now, where hast thou been, Ancient?

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Measuring the City:
I have left my Brooms at the Gate here;
By this time the Porter has stole 'em to sweep out Rascals.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Brooms?

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: I have been crying Brooms all the Town over,
And such a Mart I have made, there's no Trade near it.
O the young handsome Wenches, how they twitter'd,
When they but saw me shake my Ware, and sing too;
Come hither Master Broom-man I beseech you;
Good Master Broom-man hither, cries another.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thou art a mad Fellow.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: They are all as mad as I: they all have Trades now,
And roar about the Streets like Bull-beggars.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What Company of Soldiers are there?

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: By this means I have gather'd
Above a thousand tall and hardy Soldiers,
If need be, Colonel.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: That need's come, Ancient,
And 'twas discreetly done: go, draw 'em up presently,
But without Suspicion: this Night we shall need 'em;
Let 'em be near the Court, let Putskie guide 'em;
And wait me for Occasion: here I'll stay still.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: If it fall out we are ready; if not we are scatter'd:
I'll wait you at an Inch.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Do, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Are the Soldiers still so mutinous?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: More than ever.
No Law nor Justice frights 'em: all the Town over
They play new Pranks and Gambols: no Man's Person,
Of what Degree soever, free from Abuses:
And durst they do this, (let your Grace consider)
These monstrous, most offensive things, these Villanies,
If not set on, and fed? if not by one
They honour more than you? and more aw'd by him?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Happily their own Wants.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: I offer to supply 'em.
And every Hour make Tender of their Moneys:
They scorn it, laugh at me that offer it:
I fear the next Device will be my Life, Sir;
And willingly I'll give it, so they stay there.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Do you think Lord Archas privy?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: More than thought,
I know it, Sir, I know they durst not do
These violent rude things, abuse the State thus,
But that they have a Hope by his Ambitions —

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No more; he's sent for?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Yes, and will be here sure.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Let me talk farther with you anon.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: I'll wait, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Did you speak to the Ladies?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: They'll attend your Grace presently.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How do you like 'em?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: My Eyes are too dull Judges.
They wait here, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Be you gone then: Come in, Ladies.
Welcome to th' Court, sweet Beauties; now the Court shines,
When such true Beams of Beauty strike amongst us:
Welcome, welcome, even as your own Joys welcome.
How do you like the Court? how seems it to you?
Is't not a Place created for all Sweetness?
Why were you made such Strangers to this Happiness?
Barr'd the Delights this holds? The richest Jewels
Set ne'er so well, if they're not worn to wonder,
By judging Eyes not set off, lose their Lustre:
Your Country Shades are faint; Blasters of Beauty;
The Manners like the Place, obscure and heavy;
The Rose-buds of your Beauties turn to Cankers,
Eaten with inward Thoughts; whilst there you wander.
Here, Ladies, here, you were not made for Cloisters,
Here is the Sphere you move in: here shine nobly,
And by your powerful Influence command all:
What a sweet Modesty dwells round about 'em.
And like a nipping Morn pulls in their Blossoms?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Your Grace speaks cunningly, you do not this,
I hope, Sir, to betray us; we are poor Triumphs;
Nor can our Loss of Honour add to you, Sir:
Great Men, and great Thoughts, seek things great and worthy,
Subjects to make 'em live, and not to lose 'em;
Conquests so nobly won, can never perish.
We are two simple Maids, untutor'd here, Sir;
Two honest Maids, is that a Sin at Court, Sir?
Our Breeding is Obedience, but to good things,
To vertuous and to fair: what wou'd you win on us?
Why do I ask that Question, when I have found you?
Your Preamble has pour'd your Heart out to us;
You would dishonour us; which in your Translation
Here at the Court reads thus; Your Grace would love us,
Most dearly love us; stick us up for Mistresses:
Most certain, there are thousands of our Sex, Sir,
That would be glad of this, and handsome Women,
And crowd into this Favour, fair young Women,
Excellent Beauties, Sir: When ye have enjoy'd 'em,
And suckt those Sweets they have, what Saints are these then?
What Worship have they won? what Name, you guess, Sir,
What Story added to their time, a sweet one?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: A brave spirited Wench.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: I'll tell your Grace,
And tell you true, you are deceiv'd in us two,
Extremely cozen'd, Sir: And yet in my Eye
You are the handsom'st Man I ever lookt on,
The goodliest Gentleman; take that hope with you;
And were I fit to be your Wife (so much I honour you)
Trust me I would scratch for you but I would have you
I would wooe you then.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: She amazes me:
But how am I deceiv'd?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: O we are too honest,
Believe it, Sir, too honest, far too honest,
The way that you propound too ignorant,
And there is no medling with us; for we are Fools too,
Obstinate, peevish Fools. If I would be ill,
And had a Wanton's Itch, to kick my Heels up,
I would not leap into th' Sun, and do't there,
That all the World might see me: an obscure Shade, Sir,
Dark as the Deed, there is no trusting Light with it,
Nor that that's lighter far, vain-glorious Greatness.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You will love me as your Friend?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: I will honour you,
As your poor humble Handmaid, serve and pray for you.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What says my little one; you are not so obstinate?
Lord, how she blushes! here are truly fair Souls:
Come, you will be my Love?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Good Sir be good to me,
Indeed I'll do the best I can to please you;
I do beseech your Grace: Alas, I fear you.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What shouldst thou fear?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Fie, Sir, this is not noble.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why do I stand entreating, where my Power —

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: You have no Power, at least you ought to have none
In bad and beastly things: arm'd tnus, I'll die here,
Before she suffer wrong.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Another Archas?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: His Child, Sir, and his Spirit.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I'll deal with you then,
For here's the Honour to be won: sit down, Sweet,
Prithee, Honora, sit.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Now ye intreat I will, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I do, and will deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: That's too much Kindness.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Prithee look on me.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Yes, I love to see you,
And could look an Age thus, and admire you:
Whilst you are good and temperate, I dare touch you,
Kiss your whlte Hand.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why not my Lips?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: I dare, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I do not think ye dare.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: I am no Coward.
Do you believe me now? or now? or now, Sir?
You make me blush; but sure I mean no ill, Sir:
It had been fitrer you had kiss'd me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: That I'll do too.
What hast thou wrought into me?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: I hope all Goodness:
Whilst ye are thus, thus honest, I dare do any thing,
Thus hang about your Neck, and thus doat on you;
Bless those fair Lights: Hell take me if I durst not —
But, good Sir; pardon me. Sister come hither,
Come hither, fear not, Wench; come hither, blush not,
Come kiss the Prince, the vertuous Prince. the good Prince:

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thou wilt make me—

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Sit down, and hug him softly.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Fie, Honoira,
Wanton Honoira; is this the Modesty,
The noble Chastity your on-set shew'd me,
At first Charge beaten back? Away.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Thank you:
Upon my Knees I pray, Heaven too may thank you;
Ye have deceiv'd me cunningly, yet nobly
You have cozen'd me: In all your hopeful Life yet,
A Scene of greater Honour you ne'er acted:
I knew Fame was a Liar, too long, and loud tongu'd,
And now I have found it: O my vertuous Master!

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: My vertuous Master too.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Now you are thus,
What shall become of me let Fortune cast for't.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I'll be that Fortune, if I live, Honoira;
Thou hast done a Cure upon me, Counsel could not.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Here take your Ring, Sir, and whom you mean to ruine,
Give it to her next; I have paid for't dearly.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: A Ring to her?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why frowns my fair Alinda?
I have forgot both these again.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Stand still, Sir,
Ye have that violent killing Fire upon you,
Consumes all Honour, Credit, Faith.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: My Royal Mistress's Favour towards me,
Wo-worth you, Sir, you have poison'd, blasted.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I, Sweet?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You have taken that unmanly Liberty,
Which in a worse Man is vain-glorious feigning,
And kill'd my Truth.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Upon my Life 'tis false, Wench.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Ladies,
Take heed, ye have a cunning Gamester,
A handsome, and a high; come stor'd with Antidotes,
He has Infections else will fire your Bloods.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Prithee, Alinda, hear me.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Words steept in Honey,
That will so melt into your Minds, buy Chastity
A thousand ways, a thousand Knots to tie you;
And when he has bound you his, a thousand Ruins.
A poor lost Woman you have made me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I'll maintain thee,
And nobly too.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That Gin's too weak to take me:
Take heed, take heed, young Ladies; still take heed,
Take heed of Promises, take heed of Gifts,
Of forced feigned Sorrows, Sighs, take heed.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: By all that's mine, Alinda —

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Swear
By your Mischiefs:
O whither shall I go?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Go back again,
I'll force her take thee, love thee.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Fare you well, Sir,
I will not curse you; only this dwell with you,
When ever you love, a false Belief light on you.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: We'll take our leaves too, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Part all the World now,
Since she is gone.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: You are crooked yet, dear Master,
And still I fear —

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I am vex'd,
And some shall find it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis strange
To me to see the Court, and welcome:
O Royal Place, how have I lov'd and serv'd thee?
Who lies on this side, know'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: The Lord Burris.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Thou hast nam'd a Gentleman
I stand much bound to.
I think he sent the Casket, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: The same, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: An honest minded Man, a noble Courtier:
The Duke made perfect Choice when he took him:
Go you home, I shall hit the way
Without a Guide now.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: You may want something, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Only my Horses,
Which after Supper let the Groom wait with:
I'll have no more Attendance here.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Your Will, Sir?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: You are well met here, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: How now, Boy,
How do'st thou?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I should ask
You that Question: how do you, Sir?
How do you feel your self?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Why, well and lusty.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What do you here then?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Why, I am sent for
To Supper with the Duke.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Have you no Meat at home?
Or do you long to feed as hunted Deer do,
In Doubt and Fear?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I have an excellent Stomach,
And can I use it better
Than among my Friends, Boy?
How do the Wenches?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They do well enough, Sir,
They know the worst by this time. Pray be rul'd, Sir,
Go home again; and if you have a Supper,
Eat it in quiet there: This is no Place for you,
Especially at this time,
Take my Word for't.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: May be they'll drink hard;
I could have drank my share, Boy.
Though I am old, I will not out.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I hope you will.
Hark in your Ear: the Court's
Too quick of hearing.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Not mean me well?
Thou art abus'd and cozen'd.
Away, away.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: To that end, Sir, I tell you.
Away, if you love your self.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Who dare do these things,
That ever heard of Honesty?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Old Gentleman,
Take a Fool's Counsel.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis a Fool's indeed;
A very Fool's: thou hast more of
These Flams in thee, these musty Doubts:
Is't fit the Duke send for me,
And honour me to eat within his Presence,
And I, like a tall Fellow, play at bo-peep
With his Pleasure?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Take heed
Of bo-peep with your Pate, your Pate, Sir;
I speak plain Language now.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: If 'twere not here,
Where Reverence bids me hold,
I would so swinge thee, thou rude,
Unmanner'd Knave; take from his Bounty,
His Honour that he gives me, to beget
Sawcy and sullen Fears?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: You are not mad sure:
By this fair Light, I speak
But what it whisper'd,
And whisper'd for a Truth.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: A Dog: drunken People,
That in their Pot see Visions,
And turn States, Mad-men and Children:
Prithee do not follow me;
I tell thee I am angry:
Do not follow me.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am as angry
As you for your Heart.
I and wilful too: go, like a Woodcock,
And thrust your Neck ith' noose.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Ile kill thee.
And thou speak'st but three words more.
Do not follow me.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: A strange old foolish Fellow: I shall hear yet,
And if I do not my part hiss at me.

speeches.speaker: 1. Ser.
verse: Believe me Fellow here will be lusty drinking.
Many a washt Pate in Wine I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: 2. Serv.
verse: I am glad the old General's come: upon my conscience
That joy will make half the Court drunk. Hark the Trumpet,
They are coming on; away.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: We'll have a Rowse too.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Come seat your selves: Lord Archas sit you there,

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis far above my worth.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Ile have it so:
Are all things ready?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: All the Guards are set,
The Court Gates shut.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Then do as I prescrib'd you.
Be sure no further.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: I shall well observe you.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Come bring some Wine: here's to my Sister Gentlemen;
A Health, and much to all.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Pray fill it full Sir.
'Tis a high Health to Vertue: here Lord Burris,
A Maiden Health: you are more fit to pledge it,
You have a Maiden Soul, and much I honour it.
Passion o' me, you are sad Man.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How now Burris.
Go to, no more of this.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Take the Rowse freely.
'Twill warm your Blood, and make you fit for jollity.
Your Graces Pardon: when we get a Cup Sir,
We old Men prate a pace.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Mirth makes a Banquet;
As you love me no more.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I thank your Grace.
Give me it; Lord Borosky.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: I have ill Brains Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Damnable ill, I know it.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: But Ile pledge Sir
This vertuous Health.

speeches.speaker: Bu.
verse: The more unfit for thy Mouth.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come, bring out Robes, and let my guests look nobly,
Fit for my Love and Presence: begin downward.
Off with your Cloaks, take new.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Your Grace deals truly
Like a munificent Prince, with your poor Subjects,
Who would not fight for you? what cold dull Coward
Durst seek to save his Life when you would ask it?
Begin a new Health in your new Adornments,
The Dukes, the Royal Dukes: ah, what have I got
Sir? ah! the robe of Death!

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: You have deserv'd it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: The Livery of the Grave? do you start all from me?
Do I smell of Earth already? Sir look on me,
And like a Man; is this your Entertainment?
Do you bid your worthiest Guests to bloody Banquets.
A Guard upon me too? this is too foul play
Boy to thy good, thine Honour; thou wretched Ruler,
Thou Son of Fools and Flatterers, Heirs of Hypocrites,
Am I serv'd in a Hearse that sav'd you all?
Are you Men or Devils? do you gape upon me,
Wider, and swallow all my Services?
Entomb them first, my Faith next, then my Integrity,
And let these stuggle with your mangy Minds,
Your sear'd, and seal'd up Consciences, till you burst.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: These words are Death.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: No those Deeds that want rewards, Sirrah,
Those Battles I have fought, those horrid Dangers,
Leaner then Death, and wilder then Destruction,
I have march'd upon, these honour'd Wounds, times Story,
The Blood I have lost, the Youth, the Sorrows suffer'd,
These are my death, these that can n'er be recompenc'd,
These that you sit a brooding on like Toads,
Sucking from my Deserts the Sweets and Favours,
And render me no pay again but Poisons.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: The proud vain Soldier thou hast set—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Thou lyest.
Now by my little time of Life lyest basely,
Malitiously and loudly: how I scorn thee?
If I had sweld the Soldier, or intended
An Act in Person, leaning to dishonour,
As you would fain have forced me, witness Heaven,
Where clearest understanding of all Truth is,
(For these are spightful Men, and know no piety)
When Olin came, grim Olin, when his Marches,
His last Incursions made the City sweat,
And drove before him, as a Storm drives Hail,
Such showers of frosted Fears, shook all your Heart-strings;
Then when the Volga trembled at his Terror,
And hid his seven curl'd Heads, afraid of brusing,
By his arm'd Horses Hoofs; had I been false then,
Or blown a treacherous fire into the Soldier,
Had but one spark of Villany liv'd within me,
Ye'ad had some shadow for this black about me.
Where was your souldiership? why went not you out?
And all your right honourable Valour with you?
Why met you not the Tartar, and defi'd him?
Drew your dead doing Sword, and buckl'd with him?
Shot through his Squadrons like a fiery Meteor?
And as we see a dreadful clap of Thunder
Rend the stiff hearted Oaks, and toss their Roots up:
Why did not you so charge him? you were sick then,
You that dare taint my Credit, slipt to Bed then,
Stewing and fainting with the Fears you had,
A whorson shaking fit opprest your Lordship:
Blush Coward knave, and all the World hiss at thee.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Exceed not my command.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: I shall observe it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Are you gone too? Come weep not honest Burris,
Good loving Lord, no more Tears: 'tis not his Malice,
This Fellow's Malice, nor the Duke's Displeasure,
By bold bad Men, crowded into his Nature,
Can startle me: Fortune ne'er raz'd this Fort yet:
I am the same, the same Man, living, dying;
The same Mind to 'em both, I poize thus equal;
Only the Jugling way that told me to it,
The Judas way, to kiss me, bid me welcome,
And cut my Throat, a little Sticks upon me.
Farwel, commend me to his Grace, and tell him,
The World is full of Servants, he may have many:
And some I wish him honest: he's undone else:
But such another doating Archas never,
So try'd and touch'd a Faith: farewel for ever.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Be strong my Lord: you must not go thus lightly.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Now what's to do? what says the Law unto me?
Give me my great Offence that speaks me guilty,

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Laying aside a thousand petty Matters,
As Scorns and Insolencies, both from your self and followers,
Which you put first fire to, and these are deadly,
I come to one main Cause, which though it carries
A Strangeness in the Circumstance, it carries Death too,
Not to be pardon'd neither: you have done a Sacrilege.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: High Heaven defend me Man: how, how Borosky?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: You have took from the Temple those vow'd Arms,
The holy Ornament you hung up there,
No absolution of your Vow, no order
From Holy Church to give 'em back unto you
After they were purified from War, and rested
From Blood, made clean by Ceremony: from the Alta
You snatch'd 'em up again, again you wore 'em,
Again you stain'd 'em, stain'd your Vow, the Church too,
And rob'd it of that right was none of yours Sir,
For which the Law requires your Head, you know it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Those Arms I fought in last?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: The same.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: God a Mercy,
Thou hast hunted out a notable Cause to kill me:
A Subtle one: I dye, for saving all you;
Good Sir remember if you can, the Necessity,
The suddainness of Time, the Stage all stood in;
I was entreated to, kneel'd to, and pray'd to,
The Duke himself, the Princes, all the Nobles,
The cries of Infants, bedrid Fathers, Virgins;
Prethee find out a better Cause, a handsomer,
This will undo thee too: People will spit at thee,
The Devil himself would be asham'd of this Cause;
Because my haste made me forget the Ceremony;
The present danger every where, must my life satisfie?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: It must and shall.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: O base ungrateful People,
Have you no other Sword to cut my Throat with
But mine own nobleness? I confess, I took 'em,
The Vow not yet absolv'd, I hung em up with:
Wore 'em, fought in 'em, gilded 'em again
In the fierce Tartars Blood; for you I took 'em,
For your peculiar safety, Lord, for all,
I wore 'em for my Countries Health, that gron'd then:
Took from the Temple, to preserve the Temple,
That Holy Place, and all the Sacred Monuments,
The reverent shrines of Saints, ador'd and honour'd,
Had been consum'd to Ashes, their own Sacrifice,
Had I been slack, or staid that Absolution,
No Priest had liv'd to give it; my own Honour
Cure of my Country murder me?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: No, no Sir,
I shall force that from you, will make this cause light too,
Away with him: I shall pluck down that Heart Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Break it thou may'st; but if it bend, for pity;
Dogs and Kites eat it: come, I am Honours Martyr.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Exceed my Warrant?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: You know he loves him not.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: He dares as well meet Death as do it, eat Wildfire;
Through a few Fears I mean to try his goodness,
That I may find him fit to wear, here Burris;
I know Borosky hates him, to Death hates him,
I know he's a Serpent too, a swoln one
But I have pull'd his Sting out; what noise is that?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Down with 'em, down with the Gates.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Stand, stand, stand.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Fire the Palace before ye.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Upon my Life the Soldier, Sir, the Soldier,
A miserable time is come.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: O save him,
Upon my Knees, my hearts Knees, save Lord Archas,
We are undone else.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Dares he touch his Body?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: He racks him fearfully, most fearfully.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Away Burris,
Take Men, and take him from him; clap him up,
And if I live, I'll find a strange Death for him:
Are the Soldiers broke in?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: By this time sure they, are Sir,
They beat the Gates extreamly, beat the People.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Get me a Guard about me: make sure the Lodgings,
And speak the Soldiers fair.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Pray Heaven that take Sir.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Give us the General, we'll fire the Court else,
Render him safe and well,

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Do not fire the Cellar,
There's excellent Wine in't, Captain, and though it be cold weather,
I do not love it mull'd: bring out the General,
We'll light you, such a Bonfire else; where are you?
Speak, or we'll toss your Turrets, peep out of your Hives
We'll smoak you else: is not that a Nose there?
Put out that Nose again, and if thou dar'st
But blow it before us: now he creeps out on's Burrough.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Give us the General.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Yes, Gentlemen;
Or any thing you can desire.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: You Musk-cat
Cordevan-skin, we will not take your answer.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Where is the Duke? speak suddenly and send him hither.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Or we'll so fry your Buttocks.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Good sweet Gentlemen —

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: We are neither good, nor sweet, we are Soldiers
And you Miscreants that abuse the General,
Give fire my Boys 'tis a dark Evening,
Let's light 'em to their Lodgings.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Good Brother be not fierce.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I will not hurt her,
Fear not sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: May do what you please Sir,
I have a Sorrow that exceeds all yours,
And more, contemns all danger.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Where is the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: He's here; what would you Soldiers? wherefore troop ye
Like mutinous Mad-men thus?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Give me my Father.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Anc. Give us our General.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Set him here before us,
You see the Pledge we have got; you see these Torches;
All shall to Ashes, as I live, immediately,
A thousand lives for one.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: But hear me?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: No, we come not to dispute.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: By Heaven I swear he's rackt and whipt.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: O my poor Father!

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Burn, kill and burn.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Hold, hold I say: hold Soldiers,
On your Allegiance hold.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: We must not.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Hold:
I swear by Heaven he is a barbarous Traitor stirs first,
A Villan, and a Stranger to Obedience,
Never my Soldier more, nor Friend to honour:
Why did you use your old Man thus? thus cruelly
Torture his poor weak Body? I ever lov'd you.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Forget me in these wrongs, most noble Archas.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I have blame enough for all my hurts: weep no more Sir,
A Satisfaction for a thousand Sorrows:
I do believe you innocent, a good Man,
And Heaven forgive that naughty thing that wrong'd me.
Why look you wild my Friends? why stare you on me?
I charge you as you are Men, my Men, my Lovers,
As you are honest faithful Men, fair Soldiers,
Let down your Anger: Is not this our Soveraign,
The Head of Mercy and of Law? who dares then,
But Rebels scorning Law, appear thus violent?
Is this a place for Swords? for threatning Fires?
The Reverence of this House dares any touch,
But with obedient Knees, and pious Duties?
Are not we all his Subjects? all sworn to him?
Has not he power to punish our Offences?
And not we daily fall into 'em? assure your selves
I did offend and highly, grievously,
This good sweet Prince I offended, my Life forfeited,
Which yet his Mercy, and his old Love met with,
And only let me feel his light Rod this way:
You are to thank him for your General,
Pray for his Life, and Fortune: sweat your Bloods for him.
You are Offenders too, daily Offenders,
Proud Insolencies dwell in your Hearts, and you do 'em,
Do 'em against his Peace, his Law, his Person;
You see he only Sorrows for your Sins,
And where his Power might persecute, forgives you:
For shame put up your Swords, for honesty,
For orders sake and whose you are, my Soldiers,
Be not so rude.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They have drawn Blood from you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: That was the Blood rebel'd, the naughty Blood,
The proud provoking Blood; 'tis well 'tis out Boy;
Give you example first; draw out, and orderly.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Good Brother do

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Honest and high Example,
As thou wilt have my Blessing follow thee,
Inherit all mine Honours: thank you Theodore,
My worthy Son.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: If harm come, thank your self Sir;
I must obey you.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Captain, you know the way now:
A good Man, and a valiant; you were ever,
Inclin'd to honest things: I thank you Captain.
Souldiers, I thank you all: and love me still,
But do not love me so to lose Allegiance,
Love that above your lives: once more I thank you.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Bring him to rest, and let our Cares wait on him;
Thou excellent old Man, thou top of honour,
Where Justice and Obedience only build,
Thou stock of Vertue, how am I bound to love thee?
In all thy noble ways to follow thee?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Rememember him that vext him Sir,

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Remember!
When I forget that Villany, and to pay him
For all his mischiefs, may all good thoughts forget me

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I am very sore,

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Bring him to bed with ease Gentlemen,
For every strip Ile drop a tear to wash 'em,
And in my sad Repentance—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis too much,
I have a Life yet left to gain that Love Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: HOW do's Lord Archas yet?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: But weak an't please you,
Yet all the helps that Art can, are applied to him;
His Heart's untouch'd, and whole yet; and no doubt Sir,
His Mind being sound, his Body soon will follow.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: O that base Knave that wrong'd him, without leave too;
But I shall find an Hour to give him thanks for't;
He's fast I hope?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: As fast as Irons can keep him:
But the most fearful wretch—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: He has a Conscience,
A cruel stinging one I warrant him,
A loaden one: But what news of the Soldiers?
I did not like their parting, 'twas too sullen.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: That they keep still, and I fear a worse clap:
They are drawn out of the Town, and stand in Counsels,
Hatching unquiet Thoughts, and cruel Purposes:
I went my self unto 'em, talk'd with the Captains,
Whom I found fraught with nothing but loud Murmurs,
And desperate Curses, sounding these words often
Like Trumpets to their Angers: we are ruin'd,
Our Services turn'd to Disgraces, Mischiefs,
Our brave old General, like one had pilfer'd,
Tortur'd and whipt: the Colonel's Eyes like Torches,
Blaze every where and fright fair Peace.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Yet worse Sir:
The News is currant now, they mean to leave you,
Leave their Allegiance: and under Olins charge
The bloody Enemy march strait against you.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I have heard this too, Sir:

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: This must be prevented,
And suddenly, and warily.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: 'Tis time, Sir,
But what to minister, or how?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Go in with me,
And there we'll think upon't: such Blows as these,
Equal Defences ask, else they displease.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Lord, what a Coile has here been with these Soldiers?
They are cruel Fellows.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: And yet methought we found 'em
Handsome enough; I'll tell thee true, Petesca,
I look'd for other manner of Dealings from 'em,
And had prepar'd my self; but where's my Lady?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: In her old Dumps within; monstrous melancholy;
Sure she was mad of this Wench.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: If she had been a Man,
She would have been a great deal madder, I am glad she is shifted.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Twas a wicked thing for me to betray her,
And yet I must confess she stood in our Lights.
What young thing's this?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Good morrow beauteous Gentlewomen:
Pray you is the Princess stirring yet?

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: He has her Face.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Her very Tongue, and Tone too; her Youth upon him.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I guess you to be the Princess's Women.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Yes, we are, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Pray is there not a Gentlewoman waiting on her Grace,
You call Alinda?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: The Devil sure in her shape.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: I have heard her tell my Lady of a Brother,
An only Brother that she had: in Travel —

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Mass, I remember that: this may be he too:
I would this thing would serve her.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: So would I, Wench,
We should love him better sure: Sir, here's the Princess,
She best can satisfie you.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How I love that Presence!
O blessed Eyes, how nobly shines your Comforts!

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: What Gentleman is that?

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: We know not, Madam:
He ask'd us for your Grace: and as we guess it,
He is Alinda's Brother.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Ha! let me mark him:
My Grief has almost blinded me: her Brother!
By Venus, he has all her Sweetness upon him:
Two silver drops of Dew were never liker.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Gracious Lady —

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: That pleasant Pipe he has too.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Being my Happiness to pass by this way,
And having, as I understand by Letters,
A Sister in your vertuous Service, Madam —

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: O now my Heart, my Heart akes.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: All the Comfort
My poor Youth has, all that my Hopes have built me,
I thought it my first Duty, my best Service
Here to arrive first, humbly to thank your Grace
For my poor Sister, humbly to thank your Nobleness,
That bounteous Goodness in you.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: 'Tis he certainly.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That Spring of Favour to her: with my Life, Madam,
If any such most happy Means might meet me,
To shew my Thankfulness.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: What have I done, Fool?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: She came a Stranger to your Grace, no Courtier;
Nor of that curious Breed befits your Service;
Yet one, I dare assure my Soul, that lov'd you
Before she saw you; doated on your Vertues;
Before she knew those fair Eyes long'd to read 'em.
You only had her Prayers, you her Wishes;
And that one Hope to be yours once, preserv'd her,

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I have done wickedly.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: A little Beauty,
Such as a Cottage breeds, she brought along with her;
And yet our Country-eyes esteem'd it much too:
But for her beauteous Mind, forget, great Lady,
I am her Brother, and let me speak a Stranger:
Since she was able to beget a Thought, 'twas honest,
The daily Study how to fit your Services,
Truly to tread that vertuous Path you walk in,
So fir'd her honest Soul, we thought her Sainted;
I presume she is still the same: I would fain see her;
For, Madam, 'tis no little Love I owe her.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Sir, such a Maid there was, I had —

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: There was, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: O my poor Wench: Eyes, I will ever curse you
For your Credulity, Alinda.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That's her Name, Madam,

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Give me a little leave, Sir, to lament her.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Is she dead, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Dead, Sir, to my Service.
She is gone, pray ask me no farther.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I obey, Madam:
Gone? now must I lament too: said you gone, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Gone, gone for ever.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That's a cruel Saying:
Her Honour too?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Prithee look angry on me,
And if thou ever lovedst her, spit upon me;
Do something like a Brother, like a Friend,
And do not only say thou lov'st her —

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You amaze me.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I ruin'd her, I wrong'd her, I abus'd her;
Poor innocent Soul, I flung her; sweet Alinda,
Thou vertuous Maid, my Soul now calls thee vertuous.
Why do ye not rail now at me?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: For what, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Call me base treacherous Woman.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Heaven defend me.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Rashly I thought her false, and put her from me,
Rashly, and madly I betray'd her Modesty,
Put her to wander, Heaven knows where; nay, more, Sir,
Stuck a black Brand upon her.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: 'Twas not well, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: 'Twas damnable; she loving me so dearly,
Never poor Wench lov'd so: Sir, believe me,
'Twas the most dutious Wench, the best Companion;
When I was pleas'd, the happiest, and the gladdest,
The modestest sweet Nature dwelt within her:
I saw all this, I knew all this, I lov'd it,
I doated on it too, and yet I kill'd it:
O what have I forsaken? what have I lost?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Madam, I'll take my leave, since she is wandring,
'Tis fit I know no rest.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Will you go too, Sir?
I have not wrong'd you yet, if you dare trust me,
For yet I love Alinda there, I honour her,
I love to look upon those Eyes that speak her,
To read that Face again, Modesty keep me,
Alinda, in that shape: but why should you trust me,
'Twas I betray'd your Sister, I undid her;
And believe me, gentle Youth, 'tis I weep for her:
Appoint what Penance you please: but stay then,
And see me perform it: ask what Honour this Place
Is able to heap on you, or what Wealth:
If following me will please you, my Care of you,
Which for your Sister's sake, for your own Goodness —

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Not all the Honour-Earth has, now she's gone, Lady,
Not all the Favour; yet if I sought Preferment,
Under your bounteous Grace I would only take it.
Peace rest upon you: one sad Tear every Day
For poor Alinda's sake, 'tis fit you pay.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: A thousand, noble Youth; and when I sleep,
Even in my silver Slumbers still I'll weep.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Have you been with 'em?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Yes, an't please your Grace,
But no Persuasion serves 'em, nor no Promise,
They are fearful angry, and by this time, Sir,
Upon their March to the Enemy.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: They must be stopt.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: I, but what Force is able? and what Leader!—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How now, have you been with Archas?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Yes, and't please you,
And told him all: he frets like a chaf'd Lyon,
And calls for his Arms, and all those honest Courtiers
That dare draw Swords.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Is he able to do any thing?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: His Mind is well enough; and where his Charge is,
Let him be ne'er so sore, 'tis a full Army.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Who commands the Rebels?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: The young Colonel,
That makes the old Man almost mad: he swears, Sir,
He will not spare his Son's Head for the Dukedom.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Is the Court in Arms?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: As fast as they can bustle,
Every Man mad to go now: inspir'd strangely,
As if they were to force the Enemy.
I beseech your Grace to give me leave.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Pray go, Sir,
And look to the old Man well; take up all fairly,
And let no Blood be spilt; take general Pardons,
And quench this Fury with fair Peace.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I shall, Sir,
Or seal it with my Service; they are Villains;
The Court is up: good Sir, go strengthen 'em,
Your Royal Sight will make 'em scorn all Dangers;
The General needs no Proof.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come, let's go view 'em.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: 'Tis known we are up, and marching: no ^ubmission,
No Promise of base Peace can cure our Maladies,
We have suffer'd beyond all Repair of Honour:
Your valiant old Man's whipt; whipt, Gentlemen,
Whipt like a Slave: that Flesh that never trembled,
Nor shrunk one Sinew at a thousand Charges;
That noble Body rib'd in Arms, the Enemy
So often shook at, and then shunn'd like Thunder,
That Body's torn with Lashes.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Let's turn Head.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Turn nothing, Gentlemen, let's march on fairly,
Unless they charge us.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Think still of his Abuses,
And keep your Angers.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: He was whipt like a Top,
I never saw a Whore so lac'd: Court School butter?
Is this their Diet? I'll dress 'em one running Banquet:
What Oracle can alter us? Did not we see him?
See him we lov'd?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: And though we did obey him,
Forc'd by his Reverence for that time, is't fit, Gentlemen?
My noble Friends, is't fit we Men, and Soldiers,
Live to endure this, and look on too?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Forward:
They may call back the Sun as soon, stay Time,
Prescribe a Law to Death, as we endure this.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They will make you all fair Promises.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: We care not.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Use all their Arts upon you.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Hang all their Arts.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: And happily they'll bring him with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: March apace then,
He is old and cannot overtake us.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Say he do.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: We'll run away with him: they shall never see him more:
The Truth is, we'll hear nothing, stop at nothing,
Consider nothing but our way; believe nothing,
Not though they say their Prayers: be content with nothing,
But the knocking our their Brains: and last, do nothing,
But ban 'em and curse 'em, till we come to kill 'em.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Remove them forwards bravely; keep your Minds whole,
And the next time we face 'em, shall be fatal.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Peace to your Grace; take rest, they are before us.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: They are, Sir, and upon the March.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Lord Burris,
Take you those Horse and coast 'em: upon the first Advantage,
If they will not slack their March, charge 'em up roundly,
By that time I'll come in.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I'll do it truly.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: How do you feel your self, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Well, I thank you;
A little weak, but Anger shall supply that.
You will all stand bravely to it?

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Whilst we have Lives, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You speak like Gentlemen; I'll make the Knaves know,
The proudest and the strongest hearted Rebel,
They have a Law to live in, and they shall have;
Beat up a-pace, by this time he is upon 'em,
And Sword, but hold me now, thou shalt play ever.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Stand, stand, stand close and sure;
The Horse will charge us.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Let 'em come on, we have Provender fit for 'em.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Here comes Lord Burris, Sir, I think to parley.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: You are welcome, noble Sir, I hope to our part.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: No, valiant Colonel, I am come to chide you,
To pity you; to kill you, if these fail me;
Fie, what Dishonour seek you? What black Infamy!
Why do you draw out thus? draw all Shame with you?
Are these fit Cares in Subjects? I command you
Lay down your Arms again, move in that Peace,
That fair Obedience you were bred in.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Charge us?
We come not here to argue.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Charge up bravely,
And hotly too, we have hot Spleens to meet you,
Hot as the Shames are offer'd us

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Look behind you,
Do you see that old Man? do you know him, Soldiers?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Your Father, Sir, believe me —

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: You know his Marches,
You have seen his Executions: is it yet Peace?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: We'll die here first.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Farewel: You'll hear on's presently.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Stay, Burris: this is too poor, too beggarly a Body
To bear the Honour of a Charge from me,
A sort of tatter'd Rebels; go provide Gallouses;
You are troubled with hot Heads, I'll cool you presently:
These look like Men that were my Soldiers
Now I behold 'em nearly, and more narrowly,
My honest Friends: where got they these fair Figures?
Where did they steal these Shapes?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: They are struck already.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Do you see that Fellow there; that goodly Rebel?
He looks as like a Captain I lov'd tenderly;
A Fellow of a Faith indeed.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: He has sham'd him.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: And that that bears the Colours there, most certain
So like an Ancient of mine own, a brave Fellow,
A loving and obedient, that believe me, Burris,
I am amaz'd and troubled: and were it not
I know the general Goodness of my People,
The Duty, and the Truth, the stedfast Honesty,
And am assur'd they would as soon turn Devils
As Rebels to Allegiance, for mine Honour.

speeches.speaker: Bu.
verse: Here needs no Wars.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I pray forgive us, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Good General forgive us, or use your Sword,
Your Words are double Death.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Good noble General.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Pray, Sir, be merciful.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Weep out your shames first,
